strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: clearly identifies and demonstrates numerical overflow issues in LogSumExp computation with concrete examples and solutions
Solid theoretical foundation: Proposition 2.4 provides clean approximation bounds with controlled accuracy; Lemma 2.7 establishes strong convexity and smoothness properties essential for optimization
Simple and practical method: requires tuning only a single scalar parameter ρ; gradient formulas are implementable and composable with existing optimization techniques
Comprehensive experimental validation: covers three distinct applications (eOT, DRO with KL, DRO with unbalanced OT) with consistent improvements across different regularization regimes
Correct mathematical development: detailed proofs in appendices appear sound; thoughtful handling of convex analysis and variational formulations
Useful theoretical insights: connection to CVaR (Proposition 2.6) and safe KL divergence properties provide additional perspective on the approximation
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: the approximation coincides with Bouchard (2007) for ρ=1; related functional appeared in Soma & Yoshida (2020); the safe KL divergence is a relatively straightforward modification of standard KL divergence

Critical accuracy-smoothness trade-off unresolved: small ρ improves accuracy but degrades smoothness (requiring smaller step sizes); large ρ improves smoothness but introduces approximation error; no principled method for selecting ρ is provided, with choice appearing problem-dependent

Missing convergence analysis: paper establishes approximation properties but lacks convergence rates for SGD on the approximated objective; impact of approximation error on final solution quality is not quantified; lacks convergence guarantees for DRO problems

Limited and potentially unfair experimental comparisons: eOT only compares against LSOT (2018); recent methods acknowledged but dismissed; different hyperparameter search ranges for proposed method vs. baselines; some standard deviations very large making statistical significance unclear (e.g., Table 1: 21.2±9.8)

Modest practical improvements: for DRO with KL (Table 1), improvements diminish for large batch sizes; main advantage appears to be numerical stability rather than optimization efficiency; Table 1 shows 'no results displayed in bold' for some configurations where all approaches perform similarly

Hyperparameter selection without guidance: no systematic sensitivity analysis for ρ; no algorithm pseudocode or clear implementation guidance; incomplete sentence about code availability raises reproducibility concerns; ρ appears to require problem-specific tuning

Limited experimental scope: datasets relatively small (MNIST, EMNIST, 20K California housing); no wall-clock time comparisons or computational cost analysis; no large-scale experiments demonstrating scalability of the approach

Missing practical guidance: no guidance on when to use this method vs. alternatives; no discussion of failure modes or worst-case scenarios; conditions like F(2φ;μ)<∞ in Proposition 2.4(iii) are non-trivial but not prominently discussed

strengths: Addresses a real practical problem: numerical overflow in LogSumExp computation with small regularization parameters, with concrete examples and clear motivation
Sound theoretical framework with proper approximation bounds (F - O(ρ) ≤ Fρ ≤ F), convergence guarantees (Theorem 2.9), and preservation of convexity/smoothness properties
General-purpose approach applicable across multiple problem domains (continuous eOT, KL-DRO, UOT-DRO) without problem-specific modifications
Unbiased gradient estimators with controlled second moments, avoiding batch-size-dependent bias present in naive sampled LogSumExp approaches
Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple runs, standard deviations reported, and additional metrics beyond objectives (Table 3)
Well-organized presentation with sound mathematical exposition and extensive appendices with proofs and additional experiments
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core approximation using SoftPlus instead of exponentials closely mirrors Soma & Yoshida (2020)'s CVaR approximation; the Safe KL divergence is primarily its dual formulation rather than a fundamentally new concept
Unsolved parameter tuning problem: ρ requires manual tuning across all experiments without principled selection procedure or adaptive mechanism, significantly limiting practical appeal

Mixed experimental results: improvements are often marginal; Table 1 shows no benefit at large batch sizes; Table 2 has high variances; Table 5 shows baseline achieves higher accuracy despite better DRO objectives
Incomplete characterization of when the method matters: overflow occurs only when ε is small AND gradients are large; limited discussion of how frequently this scenario occurs in practice
Approximation error cannot be eliminated: O(ρ) error term in Theorem 2.9 means users must accept approximation gap or sacrifice convergence speed; no free lunch offered

Theory-practice gaps: computing κ̂ in practice not discussed; convergence rate depends on problem-dependent κ̂ without guidance on typical values; stepsize selection procedure not fully specified for practitioners
Limited computational complexity analysis: overhead from additional log and exponential evaluations in equation (12) not quantified; no wall-clock time comparisons provided in most experiments

Experimental design issues: grid search for learning rates with incomplete specifications; inner maximization uses only 5 iterations without sensitivity analysis; no statistical significance testing despite often small differences
